pos: n. (a son of Abishur and Abihail in the line of Jerahmeel; named once)
etymology: Hebrew 'Achban, brother of an intelligent one, or brother of understanding, from 'ach, a brother, and a root meaning to discern; named once in Scripture, at 1 Chronicles 2:29.
biblical_def: Ahban is named once, in the Jerahmeelite branch of Judah's register: “And the name of the wife of Abishur was Abihail, and she bare him Ahban, and Molid” (1 Chronicles 2:29). His name is generally read as brother of understanding. The verse is unusual for naming the mother, which the Chronicler does only where he has reason; Abihail means my father is strength, and she is given her name in a register that mostly moves father to son. The line runs through Onam and Shammai: “And the sons of Onam were, Shammai, and Jada. And the sons of Shammai; Nadab, and Abishur” (1 Chronicles 2:28). And the verse immediately after Ahban's records a death that closed a branch: “And the sons of Nadab; Seled, and Appaim: but Seled died without children” (1 Chronicles 2:30). That is the honest texture of these chapters. Some lines go forward, some stop; a man is remembered for a name and a brother, another is remembered for dying childless. The Chronicler sets both down, because the covenant runs through real households in which some sons live and some do not.

corruption_summary: The genealogies are read as uniformly triumphal, when they record childless deaths and broken branches with the same plainness as they record succession.
corruption_paragraphs: “Seled died without children” sits one verse after Ahban's birth. The Chronicler is not building a monument to unbroken success; he is keeping a record, and the record includes the lines that ended. A believer reading his own family's losses into Scripture will find them already there, written without euphemism and without despair.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God's covenant purpose runs through ordinary households where some branches flourish and some fail, and that He names the mother as readily as the father when it serves His record.

pos: n. (a son of Japhlet in the line of Asher; named once)
etymology: Hebrew 'Ashvath, of uncertain meaning, perhaps wrought or made smooth; named once in Scripture, at 1 Chronicles 7:33.
biblical_def: Ashvath is named once, at the end of a short Asherite household: “And the sons of Japhlet; Pasach, and Bimhal, and Ashvath. These are the children of Japhlet” (1 Chronicles 7:33). The register opens the tribe three verses earlier: “The sons of Asher; Imnah, and Isuah, and Ishuai, and Beriah, and Serah their sister” (1 Chronicles 7:30), and works down through Beriah and Heber: “And Heber begat Japhlet, and Shomer, and Hotham, and Shua their sister” (1 Chronicles 7:32). Asher was the tribe Jacob blessed with fatness and royal dainties and which Judges rebuked for sitting still at the shore; and yet the Chronicler's verdict on these households is anything but contemptuous: “All these were the children of Asher, heads of their father's house, choice and mighty men of valour, chief of the princes. And the number throughout the genealogy of them that were apt to the war and to battle was twenty and six thousand men” (1 Chronicles 7:40). Ashvath is one of the names that twenty-six thousand fighting men came from. The register also keeps the sisters, Serah and Shua, which is the Chronicler's habit and not an accident.

corruption_paragraphs: Asher is remembered chiefly for Deborah's rebuke that he continued on the sea shore. The Chronicler, writing long after, calls these same families choice and mighty men of valour and counts twenty-six thousand of them apt to the war. Scripture will not let a single rebuke become a people's permanent character. A tribe that failed once produced princes, and the register says so.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God keeps the sisters' names beside the sons' and the lesser tribe's honour beside the greater, and that one failure in a people's history is not its final description.

pos: n. (a son of Japhlet in the line of Asher; named once)
etymology: Hebrew Bimhal, of uncertain meaning, perhaps circumcised or by the circumcision; named once in Scripture, at 1 Chronicles 7:33.
biblical_def: Bimhal is named once, between his two brothers: “And the sons of Japhlet; Pasach, and Bimhal, and Ashvath. These are the children of Japhlet” (1 Chronicles 7:33). The Hebrew is obscure; one old reading takes it as containing the word for circumcision, which would make his name a confession of the covenant sign cut into his flesh on the eighth day. He stands in the Asherite register, descended through Beriah and Heber: “And Heber begat Japhlet, and Shomer, and Hotham, and Shua their sister” (1 Chronicles 7:32), the tribe having been opened at “The sons of Asher; Imnah, and Isuah, and Ishuai, and Beriah, and Serah their sister” (1 Chronicles 7:30). What the Chronicler finally says of all these households is the sentence worth carrying away: “All these were the children of Asher, heads of their father's house, choice and mighty men of valour, chief of the princes” (1 Chronicles 7:40). Three brothers in one verse, one of them possibly named for the covenant sign, and the whole clan reckoned among the chief of the princes. The covenant was never a thing for great men only; it was cut into infants in households like Japhlet's.

corruption_summary: The covenant sign is thought of as a national badge rather than as the mark God commanded upon the household of every believing man.
corruption_paragraphs: Circumcision in Scripture was administered in households on the eighth day, to infants who had professed nothing, as the sign and seal of a covenant God had made with their father. The dictionary holds believer's baptism as the New Testament ordinance and does not transfer the sign to infants; but it insists on reading the old sign as Scripture gives it — household-wide, God-commanded, and in the flesh — rather than as a tribal marker that happened to catch on.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God's dealings reach households, and that a man whose very name may have confessed the covenant sign is recorded among the chief of the princes.

pos: n. (a son or a town of Malchiel in the line of Asher; named once)
etymology: Hebrew Birzayith, probably the well of the olive, or olive-shaft; named once in Scripture, at 1 Chronicles 7:31.
biblical_def: Birzavith is named once: “And the sons of Beriah; Heber, and Malchiel, who is the father of Birzavith” (1 Chronicles 7:31). The name is generally read as a compound meaning the well of the olive, and in this form of Hebrew genealogy a man is often called the father of a town rather than of a son, so Birzavith is likely a place that Malchiel's house founded or held. The register opens the tribe at “The sons of Asher; Imnah, and Isuah, and Ishuai, and Beriah, and Serah their sister” (1 Chronicles 7:30), and continues down the other branch: “And Heber begat Japhlet, and Shomer, and Hotham, and Shua their sister” (1 Chronicles 7:32). Asher's portion lay in the north toward the Phoenician coast, good country for the olive, and a name meaning the well of the olive sits naturally in it. The Chronicler's closing verdict covers Birzavith with the rest: “All these were the children of Asher, heads of their father's house, choice and mighty men of valour, chief of the princes” (1 Chronicles 7:40).

corruption_summary: The idiom of Hebrew genealogy is misread, as though calling a man the father of a town were a confusion in the text.
corruption_paragraphs: Readers who come to Chronicles expecting a modern family tree are troubled when a man is called the father of a place. It is not a defect; it is the idiom, and Scripture uses it consistently — Er the father of Lecah, Malchiel the father of Birzavith, Shobal the father of Kirjath-jearim. The critical habit of treating such forms as evidence of a garbled source is unnecessary. Understand the convention and the text reads perfectly.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that Scripture speaks in the idioms of the people to whom it was first given, and that a reader's unfamiliarity is not the text's error.

pos: n. (a name borne by several in Scripture, chiefly Samuel's second son, a judge at Beersheba)
etymology: Hebrew 'Abiyah, the LORD is my father, or my father is the LORD, from 'ab, a father, and the divine name; borne by several persons in the Authorized Version.
biblical_def: Abiah is the Authorized Version's spelling for several persons, and its most consequential bearer is the second son of Samuel: “Now the name of his firstborn was Joel; and the name of his second, Abiah: they were judges in Beersheba” (1 Samuel 8:2). The name means the LORD is my father, and the man with that name is the reason Israel asked for a king. The next verse is the indictment: “And his sons walked not in his ways, but turned aside after lucre, and took bribes, and perverted judgment” (1 Samuel 8:3). The elders went to Samuel and used it: “Behold, thou art old, and thy sons walk not in thy ways: now make us a king to judge us like all the nations” (1 Samuel 8:5). The grievance was real and the remedy was sin, which is one of the hardest lessons in the historical books. The Authorized Version also gives the name to a wife of Hezron (1 Chronicles 2:24) and to a son of Becher in Benjamin: “And the sons of Becher; Zemira, and Joash, and Eliezer, and Elioenai, and Omri, and Jerimoth, and Abiah, and Anathoth, and Alameth” (1 Chronicles 7:8). Several persons, one confession of a name, and one son who did not keep it.

corruption_summary: A genuine grievance is treated as justification for a sinful remedy, which is exactly the move Israel made in 1 Samuel 8.
corruption_paragraphs: Samuel's sons were corrupt judges; the elders were not lying. And the remedy they demanded — a king like all the nations — is named by God in the same chapter as a rejection of His own kingship. This is the most common political error there is: a real abuse used to license a wrong cure. The dictionary notes it because Christians under genuine provocation are tempted to it continually.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that a man named the LORD is my father may take bribes, and that the failure of leaders is no warrant for abandoning the order God appointed.

pos: n. (an ancestor of Amashai, a priest dwelling at Jerusalem after the captivity; named once)
etymology: Hebrew 'Achzay, probably my protector, or the LORD has held fast, from a root meaning to seize or hold; named once in Scripture, at Nehemiah 11:13.
biblical_def: Ahasai is named once, two generations up a priestly pedigree in Nehemiah's register of Jerusalem: “And his brethren, chief of the fathers, two hundred forty and two: and Amashai the son of Azareel, the son of Ahasai, the son of Meshillemoth, the son of Immer” (Nehemiah 11:13). His name probably means my protector, from a root meaning to seize or hold fast. The chapter is a muster of who had settled in the rebuilt city, and it is careful with the priests: “Of the priests: Jedaiah the son of Joiarib, Jachin” (Nehemiah 11:10). The counts are given household by household — eight hundred and twenty-two who did the work of the house in one company (Nehemiah 11:12), two hundred and forty-two chiefs of the fathers in Amashai's, and then a third: “And their brethren, mighty men of valour, an hundred twenty and eight: and their overseer was Zabdiel, the son of one of the great men” (Nehemiah 11:14). A man named for God's holding fast appears in a list proving that God had held fast: the priesthood was back in the city, with its pedigrees intact after seventy years of exile.

corruption_summary: The survival of priestly pedigrees through the exile is taken for granted, when it is one of the plainest evidences of God's keeping of His own promises.
corruption_paragraphs: Seventy years in Babylon should have dissolved the house of Immer beyond recovery, and Nehemiah 11 lists it four generations deep. The critical instinct is to treat such lists as retrospective construction. The believing instinct is to read them as the record they claim to be, and to notice what they prove: that God preserved not only a people but the particular families through whom He had ordered worship.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God holds fast what He has promised, and that a man whose name means my protector stands in a list which is itself the proof of the protection.

pos: n. (an ancestor of Asaph the singer in the line of Gershom; named once)
etymology: Hebrew Ba'aseyah, generally read as the work of the LORD, or in the work of the LORD; named once in Scripture, at 1 Chronicles 6:40.
biblical_def: Baaseiah is named once, four generations up the pedigree of Asaph the chief singer: “The son of Michael, the son of Baaseiah, the son of Malchiah” (1 Chronicles 6:40). The name is generally read as the work of the LORD, which is a remarkable thing to find in the ancestry of the man who wrote twelve psalms. The pedigree is given because of the office: “And his brother Asaph, who stood on his right hand, even Asaph the son of Berachiah, the son of Shimea” (1 Chronicles 6:39). The Chronicler has already explained why he is tracing these lines at all: “And these are they whom David set over the service of song in the house of the LORD, after that the ark had rest” (1 Chronicles 6:31). Sung worship in Israel was not improvised; it was an appointed office with a succession, and the men who held it had their descent recorded like priests. The arrangement spanned the tabernacle and the temple: “And they ministered before the dwelling place of the tabernacle of the congregation with singing, until Solomon had built the house of the LORD in Jerusalem: and then they waited on their office according to their order” (1 Chronicles 6:32).

Worship music in Israel was an office under authority, not a platform for whoever could sing. The dictionary holds the regulative principle: what God commands in worship is required, and what He has not commanded is not permitted. A congregation that treats its music as entertainment to be curated by preference has lost the category this chapter assumes.

pos: n. (an ancestor of Joseph the husband of Mary, in Matthew's genealogy of the Christ)
etymology: Greek Achim, a Hellenised form of the Hebrew Yakin or Yehoyakim, meaning he whom the LORD establishes; named once in Scripture, at Matthew 1:14.
biblical_def: Achim is named once, in the third division of Matthew's genealogy: “And Azor begat Sadoc; and Sadoc begat Achim; and Achim begat Eliud” (Matthew 1:14). The Greek is a Hellenised form of a Hebrew name meaning he whom the LORD establishes. Nothing is known of the man beyond this verse. He belongs to the stretch of the line between the return from Babylon and the birth of Christ, for which no Old Testament record exists — which is to say that Matthew preserves names the Old Testament does not. The purpose of the whole list is declared in its first line: “The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, the son of David, the son of Abraham” (Matthew 1:1), and its destination in its sixteenth: “And Jacob begat Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus, who is called Christ” (Matthew 1:16). Note the care of that wording — Joseph is the husband of Mary, not the father of Jesus, and the virgin birth is protected in the very grammar of the genealogy. The structure is then stated: “So all the generations from Abraham to David are fourteen generations; and from David until the carrying away into Babylon are fourteen generations; and from the carrying away into Babylon unto Christ are fourteen generations” (Matthew 1:17).

corruption_summary: Matthew's genealogy is dismissed as unreliable because its later names appear nowhere else, and its careful wording about Joseph is overlooked.
corruption_paragraphs: The names between the captivity and the Christ have no Old Testament attestation, and the critical conclusion drawn from that is that Matthew invented or borrowed them. The believing conclusion is that Matthew, writing under inspiration and with access to records now lost, preserved what the Old Testament did not. The same chapter shows how exact he is: he writes Joseph the husband of Mary, breaking the pattern of begat at precisely the point where the virgin birth required it.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the Holy Ghost kept the names of men like Achim for the single purpose of establishing that Jesus is the son of David and the son of Abraham.

pos: n. (a captain of Judah under Jehoshaphat who willingly offered himself unto the LORD)
etymology: Hebrew 'Amasyah, the LORD bears or the LORD has borne a burden, from 'amas, to load or carry, and the divine name; named once in Scripture, at 2 Chronicles 17:16.
biblical_def: Amasiah is named once, and the verse gives him a commendation almost nobody else in Chronicles receives: “And next him was Amasiah the son of Zichri, who willingly offered himself unto the LORD; and with him two hundred thousand mighty men of valour” (2 Chronicles 17:16). His name means the LORD bears, from a verb meaning to load or to carry. He was one of Jehoshaphat's captains, and the muster around him is recorded by households: “And these are the numbers of them according to the house of their fathers: Of Judah, the captains of thousands; Adnah the chief, and with him mighty men of valour three hundred thousand” (2 Chronicles 17:14), and then Benjamin's contingents: “And of Benjamin; Eliada a mighty man of valour, and with him armed men with bow and shield two hundred thousand” (2 Chronicles 17:17). The whole force is described in one closing line: “These waited on the king, beside those whom the king put in the fenced cities throughout all Judah” (2 Chronicles 17:19). What distinguishes Amasiah is not the size of his command but the freeness of his consecration. He volunteered himself to the LORD, and the Holy Ghost wrote it down.

corruption_summary: Willing consecration is presumed where there is activity, when Scripture singles out one captain among many for having freely offered himself.
corruption_paragraphs: Every captain in 2 Chronicles 17 was serving, mustered, and counted. Only Amasiah is recorded as having willingly offered himself unto the LORD. The distinction is one Scripture makes often and the church makes rarely: a man may be fully engaged in the work and not have given himself to it. The Holy Ghost noticed the difference in a muster roll, which suggests He notices it still.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God accepts and records the freewill gift of a man's own self, and that a name meaning the LORD bears is fitly borne by one who volunteered to carry a burden.

pos: n. (a name borne by two men: the prince of Asher who divided the land, and a Benjamite of the house of Gera)
etymology: Hebrew 'Achihud, brother of majesty, or my brother is honour, from 'ach, a brother, and hod, majesty or honour; borne by two distinct men in the Authorized Version.
biblical_def: Ahihud is borne by two men. The first is the prince appointed to divide the inheritance for his tribe: “And the prince of the tribe of the children of Asher, Ahihud the son of Shelomi” (Numbers 34:27). His commission is given earlier in the chapter: “These are the names of the men which shall divide the land unto you: Eleazar the priest, and Joshua the son of Nun” (Numbers 34:17), with the instruction “And ye shall take one prince of every tribe, to divide the land by inheritance” (Numbers 34:18). Twelve such princes were named, Ahihud among them, so that no tribe could complain that its portion had been fixed without one of its own standing in the room. The second Ahihud is a Benjamite in a difficult verse of Chronicles: “And Naaman, and Ahiah, and Gera, he removed them, and begat Uzza, and Ahihud” (1 Chronicles 8:7). These are two men, in two tribes, centuries apart, under one name — and the name means brother of majesty. The dictionary records the distinction so that a later reader does not merge them: the prince of Asher who measured out Canaan is not the Benjamite of Gera's house.

corruption_summary: The division of Canaan is imagined as a conqueror's imposition, when Numbers 34 required a named prince of every tribe to stand in the division.
corruption_paragraphs: God did not let Eleazar and Joshua carve up the land between them. He commanded that one prince of every tribe be taken, named them all, and made the division a public act with twelve witnesses who each had an interest. That is a striking provision against the very abuse that the modern reader assumes — and it is in the text, not inferred from it.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God appoints due process in the distribution of what He gives, and that two men may bear one name without being one man.
